summaries.example: Imagine a science class testing how a toy car moves. The class does not just collect what each student sees. Students use ideas such as speed, time, and rules about motion to make one explanation that fits many observations. Marburg Neo-Kantians thought knowledge works in a similar way: thinking helps organize appearances into an objective system.
summaries.summary: Neo-Kantianism was a major philosophical movement in Germany from about 1870 until the First World War. Its thinkers looked back to Immanuel Kant, but they believed that understanding Kant meant also moving beyond him. They rejected the idea that philosophy should be either a guessing game about invisible realities or simply a branch of psychology. Instead, they used a method that asks what makes knowledge and other parts of culture possible. The Marburg school began with successful science and studied the laws and ideas that give scientific knowledge objectivity. It treated knowledge as an unfinished task that moves toward greater unity. The Southwest school studied values—standards about truth, goodness, and beauty—and argued that history has a different goal from physics. Physics looks for general laws, while history tries to understand unique events, people, and cultures. Both schools thought knowledge is not just a mirror of the world. Thinking helps shape and organize what we know.
key_ideas: Neo-Kantians wanted to learn from Kant, but they did not simply repeat everything Kant said.
They said philosophy should study the rules and ideas that make science, ethics, art, and history possible.
The Marburg school focused especially on science, laws, and the way knowledge grows.
The Southwest school focused especially on values and on how history differs from natural science.
summaries.why_it_matters: Neo-Kantianism shows how philosophers can respect science without saying that philosophy is just science or psychology. It also shows that different kinds of knowledge may need different methods. Their questions about objectivity, changing scientific ideas, values, and history still help us think carefully about how people support claims.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical movement that returned to Kant’s ideas while changing them to fit newer science and problems.
A way of asking what must be true or in place for knowledge or another activity to be possible.
Knowledge that does not depend on one person’s private opinion and can serve as a standard for truth.
The study of what people actually think or do. Neo-Kantians said philosophy should not be reduced to this study.

questions_to_think_about: Can a fact be true just because many people believe it?
Why might a scientist need ideas and rules, not only observations?
Should history use exactly the same methods as physics?
How can an explanation improve even if no one reaches a final, perfect theory?

summaries.example: Consider two physical theories that explain the same measurements. A Marburg Neo-Kantian would not say that the measurements alone automatically select one theory, because measurement already depends on mathematics and theoretical assumptions. Instead, the theories may be compared by broader standards, such as simplicity, scope, and their place within an evolving, unified system of knowledge. This illustrates both the rejection of a completely “given” experience and the search for objective norms of scientific inquiry.
summaries.summary: Neo-Kantianism was the leading German philosophical movement from approximately 1870 to 1914. Its members drew on Kant’s critical philosophy while revising it in response to the rise of modern science and the crisis of post-Hegelian philosophy. The two principal schools, Marburg and Southwest, disagreed about important matters, but shared a rejection of speculative metaphysics, psychologism, and the copy theory of knowledge. They held that philosophy should use a transcendental method: begin with an actual achievement of culture and investigate the principles that make its objective validity possible. For Marburg thinkers, the central case was modern mathematical natural science. Objectivity depends on the lawful unity of appearances, theories, and the historical development of inquiry. Knowledge therefore approaches a final, fully unified theory as an infinite task rather than reaching a completed endpoint. Their rejection of the given means that even observation and measurement depend on conceptual and theoretical structures. The Southwest school instead developed philosophy as a theory of value. It grounded objectivity in irreducible norms rather than in laws alone and distinguished factual validity from normative validity. Windelband and Rickert argued that history is not merely an imperfect natural science: it has an idiographic method aimed at unique, value-relevant individuals and events, unlike the nomothetic search for general laws. Thus Neo-Kantianism offered competing accounts of objectivity while sharing a broad project: explaining how knowledge and culture can be valid without reducing them to psychology or copying a ready-made world.
key_ideas: Both schools revived Kant while rejecting an orthodox repetition of his doctrines, including the traditional thing-in-itself and a fixed list of categories.
Both opposed psychologism: explaining what people believe or how they think does not by itself establish what they ought to believe.
The Marburg school interpreted the transcendental method through the fact of science and explained objectivity through lawful unity and the progressive development of knowledge.
Marburg thinkers rejected a fully given foundation for knowledge and emphasized that scientific concepts and theories can change radically while retaining forms of continuity.
The Southwest school treated validity as normative and extended critical philosophy to culture, including history.
For the Southwest school, physics is nomothetic because it seeks general laws, whereas history is idiographic because it constructs value-relevant concepts of unique individuals and events.
summaries.why_it_matters: The movement clarifies several enduring philosophical problems: how objective knowledge is possible, how scientific theories relate to experience, whether reason is independent of psychology, and whether the human sciences require methods different from physics. Its contrast between lawful explanation and value-guided interpretation also provides a useful framework for examining disagreements about science, history, and culture without assuming that one method fits every subject.

important_terms.definition: The revival and transformation of Kantian philosophy, especially in Germany from roughly 1870 to the First World War.
A method that begins with an established cultural fact, such as science, and identifies the conditions that make its objective validity possible.
The independence, truth, and object-directed correctness of knowledge; for Marburg thinkers, it is explained through lawful unity.
The view that philosophy or logic should study objective norms and contents rather than empirically describe mental events.
A principle that is prior in the logical or normative structure of knowledge, not an inborn mental feature or a belief shared by everyone.
The Marburg claim that no knowledge-content functions as a completely theory-free foundation; even basic measurements rely on concepts and laws.
The Southwest idea that philosophy studies the norms or values required for truth, goodness, beauty, and other valid practices.
Windelband’s distinction between sciences seeking general laws and sciences seeking understanding of unique individuals or events.

questions_to_think_about: If a belief is universal or innate, does that make it objectively valid? Why or why not?
Can measurements be theory-neutral, or do they depend on concepts and prior knowledge?
Does the Marburg account of an unfinished approach toward a final theory avoid skepticism, or create new problems?
Can historical selection be objective if historians decide which facts matter through values?
How should philosophy respond when science changes its basic concepts?

summaries.example: Suppose a school studies its own history. Students could count how often events happened and look for a general pattern. That would resemble a nomothetic approach, which seeks laws. Or they could explain why one particular event—such as the school’s founding—was important because of its connection to shared values and community life. That would resemble an idiographic approach, which studies a unique event. Southwest Neo-Kantians argued that history works more like the second approach.
summaries.summary: Neo-Kantianism was an influential German movement from about 1870 to the First World War. Its thinkers returned to Kant because they wanted a way to defend philosophy during a time of rapid scientific progress. But they did not try to copy Kant exactly. They rejected speculative metaphysics, which tries to discover unseen realities by pure reasoning, and they also rejected psychologism, the idea that psychology can explain what makes beliefs logically correct. Their shared method was called the transcendental method. It starts with something real in culture—especially science—and asks what must be true for it to count as valid knowledge. The Marburg school, associated with Hermann Cohen and Paul Natorp, focused on science. It explained objectivity through laws that connect different appearances and pieces of knowledge. Scientific knowledge is never finished, but it can move toward an ideal of complete unity. Marburg thinkers also said there is no entirely theory-free “given”: even measurements require concepts and scientific assumptions. The Southwest school, associated with Wilhelm Windelband and Heinrich Rickert, focused on values. It argued that philosophy studies norms for truth, action, and beauty. It also distinguished two scientific methods. Nomothetic sciences, such as physics, seek general laws. Idiographic sciences, especially history, seek to understand unique people, events, and cultures. Although the schools disagreed, both held that knowledge requires active thinking and principles that are not merely copied from experience.
key_ideas: Neo-Kantians followed Kant in asking how knowledge is possible, but they changed his ideas to fit modern science and culture.
Marburg and Southwest thinkers belonged to related schools, yet they criticized each other and explained objectivity differently.
Marburg philosophers began with science and emphasized laws, judgments, and the gradual unification of knowledge.
Southwest philosophers emphasized values and argued that history has its own way of knowing.
Both schools rejected the idea that knowledge is a simple copy of objects or a product of psychology alone.
summaries.why_it_matters: Neo-Kantianism helps explain why knowledge can be objective without being a photograph of reality. It also encourages us to ask whether the same standards should apply to every field. A physics experiment and a historical explanation may both be disciplined and evidence-based while having different goals. These ideas can make discussions about science, history, and values more careful.

important_terms.definition: A movement that used Kant’s philosophy as a starting point but revised it rather than accepting it unchanged.
A method that asks what conditions make something such as science or ethical judgment possible.
Being true and independent of any one person’s opinion, while serving as a standard for judging knowledge.
The mistake of treating psychology’s description of mental events as if it settled the logical or normative question of what is true.
A principle needed for knowledge or judgment, understood by Neo-Kantians as logical or normative rather than simply inborn.
The Marburg view that experience is not a completely raw foundation; even observations and measurements use concepts and theories.
The study of standards that guide truth, goodness, beauty, and other forms of cultural activity.
A method aimed at general laws, unlike an idiographic method, which aims to understand unique events or individuals.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “many people believe it” different from “it is objectively valid”?
Do observations always depend on ideas about what to look for and how to measure?
What might history lose if it searched only for general laws?
Can a theory improve even when scientists do not yet have a final explanation?
Which seems more convincing: explaining objectivity through laws or through values?
